stories.title: US to livestream execution of Fort Hood mass shooter
stories.summary: The US will livestream the army's upcoming firing squad execution of a man who ⁠killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon has said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. Nidal Hasan, a former US army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945. The execution is scheduled for 3 December at the same Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the failed execution by injection of a Tennessee woman last week. "It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post.

stories.title: O'Loan resisted pressure over Omagh bomb report - inquiry
stories.summary: Former Northern Ireland police ombudsman Nuala O'Loan resisted "high level" political pressure from the then Northern Ireland secretary not to publish her critical report into the Omagh bombing investigation, the public inquiry has heard. Martin Bridger was an investigator for the Police Ombudsman of Northern Ireland at the time of its establishment in 2000 and gave evidence to the inquiry today. The dissident republican car bombing in Omagh on 15 August 1998 killed 29 people, including a woman who was pregnant with twins. In 2001, an article was released containing claims from undercover agent Kevin Fulton that he had told his RUC handlers that a car bomb was being prepared three days before the attack in Omagh. The inquiry heard that Mr Bridger was involved in initial inquiries that led the then police ombudsman Ms O’Loan to launch a full investigation into the claims. He said he met Mr Fulton once as part of those initial inquiries and a number of times later when carrying out work to persuade the UK state to establish a public inquiry into the Omagh bomb.

stories.title: Polls close in London by-election to replace Starmer
stories.summary: Polls have closed in a by-election to replace former Labour Party leader and British prime minister Keir Starmer as Holborn and St Pancras MP, with results expected to be announced in the early hours of tomorrow morning. The north London seat has been a Labour stronghold since its formation in 1983, held by Frank Dobson for 32 years and Mr Starmer for 11. However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski is hoping to break Labour's clean sheet and secure his own seat in the House of Commons. The by-election comes in a difficult week for Mr Polanski’s party, after a controversial motion was passed at the Green Party conference asserting that "Zionism is racism". Mr Polanski, who abstained on the vote, later said that he will "not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of". Labour’s candidate in the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who is the bookies’ favourite to win.

stories.title: DCC Energy to sell tech unit Nexora for $725m
stories.summary: Energy distributor DCC Energy said today it would sell its technology division, Nexora, to private equity firm One Equity Partners for a total enterprise value of $725m on a cash- and debt-free basis. The sale of the business is expected to complete on or after March 1, 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, DCC said in a statement. DCC agreed to a £5.75 billion takeover by a consortium of US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners in July. DCC said its shareholders will receive an additional 42 pence per share on top of the existing offer from the KKR-led consortium. But if regulatory conditions related to the sale of Nexora are not met by July 31, 2027, the additional consideration will be zero, it added. Donal Murphy, the chief executive of DCC Energy, said Nexora has been an important part of the DCC Group for many years and has built a strong market position through the expertise and commitment of its people.

stories.title: Thousands march in Madrid to honour pensioner Abascal
stories.summary: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose ⁠eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month. Maricarmen Abascal, who died yesterday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on 23 September. No cause of death has been announced. Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis. As the sun set in Madrid, thousands followed a line of Tenants Union members, dressed in orange vests and walking arm-in-arm, as they carried a wreath of flowers from a protest camp in central Puerta del Sol square to Ms Abascal's former home near Retiro Park. "They're not deaths; they're murders," the protesters chanted. Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.

stories.title: Normality returns ahead of unpredictable weekend
stories.summary: After an international window like no other it almost feels comforting to get back to the madness of the League of Ireland. Normality, if that word can ever be associated with our league, has returned. We have a three-team title race where St Patrick's Athletic and Bohemians sit on 59 points while Shamrock Rovers sit 3 points ahead of them both after their comfortable win against Drogheda last night in Tallaght. We also have two FAI Cup semi-finals this weekend and, just to make sure things remain suitably chaotic, Derry City and James McClean are publicly at it again. And of course - Bohemians have put out a media ban due to last night's game being put back to Thursday to allow it to be televised, which gives Rovers an extra day of rest before the Dublin Derby between Rovers and Bohs on Monday. The McClean situation is an unfortunate distraction for Derry ahead of arguably their biggest game of the season. McClean has made it clear he believes he is fit and ready to play while Derry have responded publicly, making the point that selection is ultimately determined by the club and its medical team.

stories.title: Mayo great Cillian O'Connor announces retirement
stories.summary: Mayo great Cillian O'Connor has announced his retirement from inter-county football at the age of 34 in the wake of the county's All-Ireland winning campaign. O'Connor, a two-time All-Star, who became the leading scorer in the history of the All-Ireland football championship in 2019, made the announcement in an extensive interview with the Irish Examiner's Maurice Brosnan. The Ballintubber forward confirmed he would not be part of the Mayo squad for the 2027 campaign. O'Connor had been a mainstay in the Mayo attack for over a decade, first breaking through as a regular starter as a 19-year old during James Horan's first year in charge. He was their primary marksman and top scorer for the remainder of the decade, during which Mayo reached four All-Ireland finals, suffering a series of agonising defeats, first to Donegal in 2012 and then to Dublin in 2013, 2016 and 2017. O'Connor surpassed Colm Cooper's all-time championship scoring record in the 2019 season and during the behind-closed-doors 2020 season, he posted another record as he racked up 4-09 in the All-Ireland semi-final victory over Tipperary, the highest ever tally registered by an individual in the championship game.

stories.title: Ireland U21s poised to learn Euro 2027 play-off opponents
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland Under-21s will learn who they have to beat to secure their place at the 2027 European Championship on Friday. Jim Crawford's side are in the pot for the play-off draw which takes place in Nyon at 10am. Ireland secured their place in the play-offs with a stunning 3-1 victory over England at Turner's Cross to finish runners-up in Group D and edge out Slovakia, who finished third and miss out on the draw. Trailing to an eighth-minute goal by Tyler Dibling, Ireland roared back with two goals from Tommy Lonergan and another from Conor McManus to book their place in the eight-country play-offs. The play-off draw is an open one and will not be seeded, meaning that Ireland can play any of the other seven teams in the draw. Czechia, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Iceland, Netherlands and Turkey are all potential opponents for the Boys in Green.

stories.title: Lenihan hopeful Lee can turn Munster's fortunes around
stories.summary: Donal Lenihan says he's hopeful that Avan Lee's appointment as the Interim CEO of Munster Rugby can help the province to turn a corner after a tumultuous period. Ian Flanagan quit the role last week in the wake of a number of controversies off the pitch, most notably the decision to appoint Roger Randle as attack coach before agreeing a mutual termination of that agreement. On the field, the team have enjoyed limited success, with their last European Cup coming back in 2008, and just one addition to the trophy cabinet - a URC title in 2023 - since 2011. "There's a massive amount of frustration within the way rugby has been run within the province," he said. "You have a lot of people who've been there for a long time and I just think Avan's appointment is like drawing a line in the sand. "I'm thrilled to think that he's an independent thinker of the game. I'd like to think that he would engage with people who have a clear understanding of what rucks down here.

stories.title: Open House Dublin - the festival of architecture returns
stories.summary: Emmett Scanlon, Director of the Irish Architecture Foundation, introduces the 2026 edition of Open House Dublin, the capital's festival of architecture, which returns this October. This year's Open House Festival explores the idea that "Dublin Is Living" and that people are its life support. On a daily basis, it is communities of place and interest, on streets, in rooms, parks and pitches, that form and shape Dublin city and county. This year we place this unique relationship between people and place front and centre at Ireland’s largest and longest running festival of architecture. Our nine-day festival invites you to explore the city and county and join a conversation about our capital's future. More than 200 free events are taking place, from behind-the-scenes tours to talks, workshops and exhibitions. People of all ages, backgrounds and abilities can discover Dublin and consider what it means to live, thrive and belong here. For younger visitors, Open House Junior brings architecture to life on 10–11 October with free workshops, walking tours and creative activities for children, teenagers and families to explore and reimagine the places around them. For the first time, our 'Open Table' series will take place across all four Dublin local authority areas. Hosted by housing and urban design expert Dr Lorcan Sirr, these lunchtime conversations are a chance to share experiences, local knowledge and ideas for their neighbourhoods. From 12-15 October, in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown, Fingal, South Dublin and Dublin City, the discussions will feed into the Dublin Is Living Town Hall. Happening on the evening of Thursday 15 October at Wood Quay, the Dublin Is Living Town Hall will bring together residents, community advocates, local business owners and voices from architecture and public life to discuss the big questions facing Dublin, including housing, vacant buildings, transport, green space, safety and belonging. Perspectives gathered at the Open Tables will bring neighbourhood experiences into this wider discussion about Dublin’s future.

stories.title: Andrew Scott on 'very special' role in new film Elsinore
stories.summary: Irish actor Andrew Scott has spoken about the importance of celebrating life in the face of tragedy as his new film, Elsinore, opened the London Film Festival. The Fleabag and Ripley star plays Scottish actor Ian Charleson in the biographical drama, which had its European premiere on Wednesday night. Charleson, best known for his role in Chariots of Fire, was diagnosed with AIDS before taking on the title role in Hamlet at London's National Theatre in 1989. Scott, who also produced the film, said he wanted to celebrate Charleson’s life rather than focus solely on his final months. "I think the biggest thing for me was to understand that he was a man who had a great zest for life, and who was very funny and kind of charming and sexy and a wonderful person who was deeply loved," he told Reuters. Directed by Simon Stone, Elsinore follows Charleson as he steps into the role of Hamlet following Daniel Day-Lewis’s departure from the production.

stories.title: Why Irish designers are so drawn to the Gothic in fashion
stories.summary: Laura Fitzachary is a historian and historical content creator based in Dublin who specialises in fashion and beauty history in Ireland and beyond. Ahead of spooky season, fashion historian Laura Fitzachary explores how Gothic tropes and traditional Irish stories have Irish fashion designers enthralled. Inspired by storytelling and craftsmanship, Gothic fashion naturally finds a home in Ireland. So it is not surprising that Irish designers such as Jonathan Anderson, Dior Creative Director, and Simone Rocha have referenced Gothic literature, Irish mythology and Victorian mourning dress. A literal take on the iconic Dior Book Tote was revealed by Magherafelt-born Anderson in 2025 in the lead up Dior Homme SS '26, one of which featured an homage to the first edition of Dracula by Bram Stoker. As noted by Dior, Stoker’s Dracula take its place in Anderson’s "dream library". The Gothic horror novel was published in 1897 and draws extensively from folklore and history. While there are several theories as to who the character of 'Dracula’ is based on, this mystery has even spilled over into fashion. Alexander McQueen’s FW ‘09 Menswear featured models bearing a cane, a top hat and a coat draped over the shoulders – a direct nod to the human form of the vampire depicted by Gary Oldman in Bram Stoker’s Dracula, Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 interpretation of the novel. What is known is the strong influence of traditional Irish tales on Stoker’s writing, which has been argued by historians such as David J. Skal.

stories.title: Man shot by ICE agents with child present, Mamdani says
stories.summary: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of New York ⁠City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses. Federal immigration agents have shot at least 21 people since Donald Trump returned to office, seven fatally, sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Mr Trump's push to ramp up deportations has led to an increasing number of violent confrontations, and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved. Mr Trump has said many migrants must be deported, blaming them, often in sweeping terms, for financial fraud and violent crimes. "Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "I have been on the phone with President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary Mullin, negotiating the release of ‌the man ICE agents shot. Those negotiations were ⁠unsuccessful," Mr Mamdani said in a press conference yesterday evening.

stories.title: Garda protective disclosure unit under review, cttee told
stories.summary: Justin Kelly told the Public Accounts Committee that he has full confidence in the unit which has been strengthened in the last number of years, including the appointment of a full time manager, additional training and updated policies. Commissioner Kelly said An Garda Síochána wanted people to come forward and he was satisfied it has the processes, policies and structures in place to enable them to do so. In the past six years, 113 protected disclosures have been made, including 17 so far this year. Mr Kelly also said there was "a limited role" for him as commissioner around protected disclosures and that he had not reviewed any. In response to an allegation that the previous commissioner had interfered in a protected disclosure process, he said he had "absolutely no concern around any decision he made". He described Drew Harris as an "officer of utmost standing and integrity" who had "an impeccable career" and who sent out "a message" that criminality and breaches of discipline in An Garda Síochána would not be tolerated.

The coalition has "invested in people and services", Ms McEntee said, including Income Tax changes, Carbon Tax policies and new plans to help people retrofit their homes.

stories.title: 20 Chinese car brands to attend Paris Motor Show
stories.summary: A record 20 Chinese car brands will descend on next week's Paris Motor Show, underscoring how rapidly China's automakers have established themselves as a competitive threat in Europe despite mounting trade barriers. European carmakers will use the show to unveil new models and try to reassure investors they can compete, as Chinese rivals gain market share with a growing range of electric vehicles and hybrids. This year's Chinese contingent will be twice the size of the one at the last show in 2024, with established names such as BYD and Chery joined by newcomers including Aito and Avatr. The Paris Motor Show comes at a pivotal moment for Europe's auto industry. Sales by European manufacturers in China have slumped since the Covid-19 pandemic, while Chinese automakers, largely shut out of the US and facing weaker demand at home, have increasingly turned their attention to Europe. "The Chinese are saying 'we've got to try and dominate Europe because we can't do anything in the US'," said Brad Kunz, a partner at consultancy Grant Thornton Stax. "If the US had allowed Chinese automakers in, Europe wouldn't be so much of a battleground." Data from Schmidt Automotive Research show Chinese brands held a 10.7% share of the European market in the second quarter, up from 5.7% a year earlier and above Japanese rivals who arrived in Europe in the 1970s.

stories.title: Pike may face execution after recovery, says US doctor
stories.summary: A medical adviser to Christa Pike's legal team has said the more her condition improves, the more likely she is to eventually face execution. Christa Pike survived an execution attempt in Tennessee in the US last week. The 50-year-old survived two doses of pentobarbital as officials attempted to put her to death by lethal injection. She had been sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Yesterday, her lawyers said she was conscious and speaking as she receives treatment in hospital. "But it's clear that the more that she improves, the more likely she is to be subjected to execution in the future. That'll be up to the lawyers to debate as to what will happen. But there's nothing automatically that excludes the state from trying again," explained Dr Zivot.

stories.title: Cullen excited by return to Leinster's 'quirky' home
stories.summary: It feels like an age since Leinster last hosted a competitive game at the RDS, a URC quarter-final against Connacht in late May, 2024. Just over 26 months and a €52m redevelopment later, Leo Cullen's side will finally get to run out at what is now called the Laya Arena, which is expected to come close to hitting its 20,500 capacity for its full opening against Cardiff on Saturday. They didn't have to move far during their two seasons away. In fact, they didn't even have to leave Ballsbridge, as they set up shop at Aviva Stadium, occasionally venturing to Croke Park. The Aviva is a great place to play, but it's not home. And as they prepare for their first home game of the new season, the Leinster head coach is excited about getting back to their new and improved - but still "quirky" venue. "It's an insane amount of rugby clubs in a very small area, and then we're playing in the showjumping arena, playing rugby. "So it's an amazing thing, because obviously my mum breeds horses and ponies, as some of you may well be aware of. So I've been going there since I was literally a baby.

stories.title: New-look Leinster hurling championship set for Congress
stories.summary: A new-look Leinster senior hurling championship will be put to a vote at next year's annual GAA Congress after the provincial council’s management last night gave the green light to the proposal. The new format, featuring eight teams, looks set to be up and running by 2028, if, as expected, it gets the go-ahead at Congress next year. It has been cultivated to give emerging counties a more feasible pathway to steady and sustainable improvement by helping yo-yo counties bridge the gap with the game's top sides. The final recommendation of a Leinster workshop committee, led by former president Nickey Brennan, recommends two groups of four incorporating the Joe McDonagh Cup finalists. The recommendation has received huge support among counties and got approval from Leinster GAA management on Tuesday night. The report was requested by Leinster GAA chair Martin Byrne and aims to give tier two counties greater opportunities whilst also preserving the competitiveness of the province's flagship competition.

stories.title: Munster appoint New Zealander Lee as interim CEO
stories.summary: New Zealander Avan Lee has been appointed as interim CEO of Munster Rugby, following the resignation of chief executive Ian Flanagan las week. Flanagan confirmed last Thursday that he would be stepping down from his position at the end of October, following seven years in the role. Munster have moved swiftly to find a replacement, with Lee set to fill the role on an interim basis, although he is open to applying for the permanent position. An experienced rugby executive, Lee previously served as CEO of the Hurricanes from 2015 until the end of 2025, with the Wellington franchise winning a Super Rugby title in 2016, while they were also crowned champions just after his departure earlier this year. "I am honoured to be appointed interim CEO of Munster Rugby," the New Zealander said. "This is a province with a proud history, passionate supporters and a strong reputation within the game."

stories.title: Shared skies - artist Fergal McCarthy draws Offaly's birdlife
stories.summary: Artist Fergal McCarthy introduces Shared Skies, his new series of drawings capturing the diverse birdlife to be found on the floodplans of the Shannon Callows in Co. Offaly, currently on display in Birr Library. Some years back I read an interview with Michael Keegan Dolan, the artistic director of the celebrated dance company Teac Damsa. Inspired by the whooper swans that migrated to a lake near his house each winter from Iceland, he decided to reimagine the ballet Swan Lake with a Midlands context. I was inspired by these swans too. I had just returned from an art residency in Iceland at the time, where I worked on a project about the shared interest in myth and sagas in both our cultures. Back then, direct flights had yet to exist between Iceland and Ireland. I loved the fact that these whooper swans were connecting our two countries, drawing invisible lines across the North Atlantic and maintaining a relationship that has existed since Iceland was first populated by Irish monks. The monks were sadly driven out by the arrival of the Vikings who brought women from Ireland and Scotland with them to become their wives. To this day, up to 66% of Icelandic women can trace their ancestry to both of these countries. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from your mother, creating another somewhat invisible line of connection between Iceland and Ireland. I thought about making a short film about the 1300km journey made by the whooper swans each October. They arrive in large groups in Lough Foyle before journeying on to multiple locations across Ireland including Michael Keegan Dolan's lake in Longford and the Shannon Callows in Offaly. I drove to Lough Gara in Sligo and spent some time listening to the loud whooping and honking of these yellow-billed beauties. At a time when our borders are being increasingly monitored and controlled, I love that these extraordinary birds maintain these millennia-long connections between Europe and a floodplain in Offaly.

stories.title: Lyra releases her cover of The Pogues' Streets Of Sorrow
stories.summary: Irish singer songwriter Lyra has released her rendition of The Pogues' Streets of Sorrow/Birmingham Six from the upcoming tribute album, 20th Century Paddy - The Songs of Shane MacGowan. The Cork singer joins U2, Bruce Springsteen, Hozier, Tom Waits, The Jesus and Mary Chain, and Damien Dempsey on the 36-track homage to MacGowan who passed away in November 2023. Ahead of its release on the 13th of November, Lyra has unveiled her version of the song, co-written by MacGowan and fellow Pogue Terry Woods for the 1988 album If I Should Fall from Grace with God. The tracks were written in support of the Birmingham Six and the Guildford Four, who were the victims of a miscarriage of Justice after they were falsely imprisoned in the UK for IRA atrocities in the 1970s. Lyra, whose own songs include Falling, Chess, and Lovers, said, "Being part of this album is a huge honour. Shane had this extraordinary ability to put beauty, pain and defiance into a song, and being invited to help celebrate that as an Irish artist feels very special. She added, "What drew me to Streets of Sorrow/Birmingham Six was the way it’s written. It opens with this beautiful, sorrowful lament, and then there’s a real change in energy. Suddenly there’s fire in it.

stories.title: Polanski vows to stay Greens leader despite election loss
stories.summary: Zack Polanski has vowed to carry on as the Green Party leader for England and Wales after he failed to win a seat in Parliament in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. Mr Polanski was defeated by Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who retained the seat for Labour after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned. She secured 45% of the vote to the Greens' 33%, a majority of 3,364, but a 13% swing to the Greens, whose vote share was up by 22.4%. The vote came in a week that has seen Mr Polanski under pressure after Green members backed a motion declaring Zionism is racism, but he insisted he would stay on as leader. "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party," he said when asked about a potential threat to his leadership after the loss. "Of course, I wanted to win. No-one runs an election to lose," he said, but added that people on the doorstep had been excited about his plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water.

stories.title: Musk's X fails in court action against Comisiún na Meán
stories.summary: Elon Musk's X, formerly known as Twitter, has failed in a High Court bid challenging how the media regulator, Comisiún na Meán, deals with user complaints against social media platforms. At the High Court today, Mr Justice Cian Ferriter ruled that the commission is entitled under law to refer information from complaints made under the Digital Services Act to a 'supervisory' unit, which also has the power to retain those complaints to identify possible future compliance issues. X had submitted that the commission could not legally refer information garnered from complaints to the supervision team if those complaints were already concluded or undetermined. They also submitted that information contained within those complaints could not be used for broader, future systemic investigations and that the regulator had therefore acted outside of the law. X further submitted that it regularly takes "unilateral" removal action, such as in cases of child exploitation, which it is obligated to do by its own regulatory policies. They submitted that the commission was acting in an "extra statutory" manner.

stories.title: Budget funding not enough for public pay deal, say unions
stories.summary: The row over a public sector pay deal is continuing with unions insisting the funding on offer for such an agreement was not enough to break the deadlock. Yesterday, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers announced that he was setting aside €1.2 billion for a public sector pay deal. He also called on the Irish Congress of Trade Unions and other associations to match this intent by re-engaging as a "matter of urgency" and standing down their industrial action. However, public sector unions said the money allocated was not enough to resolve the current dispute. ICTU General Secretary Owen Reidy said the measures did not go far enough to stave off a nationwide strike by public servants planned for next Wednesday. Since last week, workers across the public sector have been engaging in industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule ahead of planned strikes on 14 October and 21 October.

stories.title: Are you due a tax refund? 3 tax credits you may not know about
stories.summary: Analysis: Thousands of taxpayers are missing out on refunds by not availing of tax credits for medical expenses, rent and college tuition fees. This article is now available as a Brainstorm podcast and can be heard above. You can also subscribe to the Brainstorm podcast through Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. While Benjamin Franklin once famously wrote "in this world nothing can be said to be certain except death and taxes", certainty is not the only thing these two have in common. Among other things, the tax world possesses its own reaper-like character, often manifesting in the shape of the dreaded "Tax Man". The prospect of having to engage with this looming spectre can create an understandable anxiety in the collective consciousness, an anxiety that is often exacerbated by the tax system itself. In Ireland most employees (whose only income source is their salary) manage to avoid ever having to engage directly with the Tax Man, namely the Revenue Commissioners. Our income tax bills are calculated and collected by our employers through payroll and passed directly to Revenue. In the past, we would have received a physical payslip, leading us to scratch our heads as to what the various figures meant. In these digital times, we seldom see any tax calculation detail, making the thoughts of engaging with Revenue even more anxiety-inducing. Fearful of the possibility of owing even more tax, we often leave well enough alone lest any contact with Revenue cost us more money. But there may well be a financial downside to this lack of engagement with Revenue. While most employers will have enough information to allocate the correct personal tax credits to their employees, some tax credits are dependent on payments made by the taxpayer themselves. As these won’t be reflected in payroll calculations, taxpayers must apply for these extra credits, or risk leaving money behind in the form of potential tax refunds. Here are three of the most underutilised tax credits.

stories.title: Canadian writer Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
stories.summary: Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical ⁠tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the award-giving body said today. The prize is awarded by the Swedish Academy and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns (€1.07m). Canadian poet and essayist Carson's work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix. She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work which ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as 'Autobiography of ‌Red' from 1998. Her style ⁠is exemplified in ‘Norma Jeane Baker of Troy’ from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides' play ‘Helen’ and Marilyn Monroe. Ms Carson said the members of the Swedish Academy were "crazy" for honouring her.

stories.title: United Rugby Championship Round 3: All You Need to Know
stories.summary: It's Round 3 of the BKT United Rugby Championship, and it feels like the season is really up and running. In the next four weekends, we have three URC Interpros down for decision, as well as a round of Investec Champions Cup, and the first of those Interpros is on Saturday evening, as Ulster host Munster up in Belfast. Ulster are without a win so far this season, but Richie Murphy's side do have five points on the board, after a draw and three bonus-points, while Munster picked up their first victory last weekend, with an impressive 26-22 bonus-point win at home to the Bulls. It's Friday night lights for Connacht for the third week in a row, as Stuart Lancaster's side face a tough away trip to Glasgow. And then on Saturday night, Leinster host Cardiff in their first competitive game back at the new and improved Laya Arena, with Leo Cullen's side looking for their first win of the season. Glasgow Warriors v Connacht (Friday, 7.45pm) and Leinster v Cardiff (Saturday, 7.45pm) are both live on TG4 and Premier Sports.
